title: CD and DVD drive: steppers, laser diode and tiny magnets
summary: Every dead CD or DVD drive holds a tiny stepper motor with a lead screw, a spindle motor, a tray motor, steel guide rods, small neodymium magnets and a laser diode. Fifteen minutes with a screwdriver. Treat the laser as an eye hazard.

steps.text: Pull the drive out of the computer or player and unplug every cable.
If the tray is shut, push a straightened paperclip into the small hole on the front panel to release it, then pull the tray out by hand.
Remove the 4 screws on the bottom or sides and lift off the steel top and bottom covers. Unclip the plastic front bezel.
steps.warn: Cover edges are sharp. Handle them by the flat faces.

steps.text: Unlatch the ribbon cables and lift out the main circuit board.
Lift out the inner frame that holds the laser sled. It is often mounted on rubber grommets; pull it free.
Remove the stepper motor: undo its 2 screws. It comes out with its lead screw attached. Keep the small bracket and screw together.
Take out the two polished steel guide rods: undo the small clips or screws at each end and slide them out of the sled.
Remove the spindle motor (2–3 screws from underneath). The disc clamp in the lid often holds a small magnet as well; pry it out.
Remove the tray motor, its rubber belt and gears from the front corner.
Pick out the focus lens: it sits on fine wires above the sled. The tiny neodymium magnets are either side of it. Pry them out with a small flat screwdriver.

To get the laser diode, desolder its 3 leads from the flex circuit, then work the small metal can out of the sled. It is often glued; heat and gentle pressure help. Twist its leads together straight away to protect it from static.
steps.warn: Never look into the diode or lens while it has any power. Burner diodes are many times stronger than a laser pointer and CD diodes are invisible infrared.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Stepper motor and lead screw.** A ready-made precise linear axis. Good for small positioning jobs, a sun tracker, a tiny plotter or a valve.
- **Spindle motor.** A small flat brushless motor. Needs a brushless driver to run, or use it as a tiny 3-phase generator.
- **Tray motor and gears.** A small 5 V brushed DC motor with a gear train. Easy to run from a USB supply.
- **Guide rods.** Short polished steel rods, about 3–4 mm across. Axles, pins, small shafts.
- **Neodymium magnets.** Very small but strong. Reed switch triggers, compass work, holding small parts.
- **Laser diode.** DVD burners carry the strongest red diodes; CD drives carry infrared ones; Blu-ray drives carry violet ones. A diode needs a current-limiting driver: connecting it straight to a battery kills it in a moment. A good diode in a driver makes a signal light or a fire-starting lens experiment at very close range only.
- **Main board.** Motor driver chips and connectors; little else.

## Variations

- Slim laptop drives have the same parts in miniature and no tray motor.
- Stand-alone players (DVD players, car CD units) add a power supply board, a display and remote-control receiver.
- Older CD-ROM drives sometimes use a DC motor and gears for the sled instead of a stepper.

## Laser safety

Light from a burner diode can burn your retina before you blink. Test only with the beam pointed at a wall, with nobody else in the room, and with goggles rated for the wavelength if you have them. Infrared diodes give no visible warning.

## What to leave

- The plastic chassis and the bezel.
- The photodiode array in the sled is too specialised to be much use.
